properties.name: Louisville and Portland Canal (locks)
properties.title: Louisville and Portland Canal (locks)
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · Louisville and Portland Canal lock site · chartered 1825 · construction 1826 · opened 1830
properties.history: The Falls of the Ohio form the only barrier to navigation between Pittsburgh and New Orleans, and cargo was portaged around them except for a few weeks of high water each spring. Kentucky chartered the private Louisville and Portland Canal Company in 1825; construction started March 1, 1826, and the canal opened in 1830. As built, it was 1.9 miles long and 64 feet wide and ended in a three-flight lock with a total lift of 26 feet. Wikipedia describes it as the first major improvement completed on a major U.S. river and dates full completion to 1833. The route was later enlarged and rebuilt and is now the McAlpine Locks and Dam canal; the pin marks the lock site at the downstream end.

properties.name: Col. John Hardin’s Pleasant Run homestead (approximate)
properties.title: Col. John Hardin’s Pleasant Run homestead (approximate)
properties.subtitle: Washington County · Pleasant Run, ~3 mi east of Springfield (approximate) · settled April 1786 · killed on 1792 peace mission
properties.history: John Hardin was born in Virginia in 1753. In August 1774, at the start of Lord Dunmore’s War, he was wounded in a skirmish at Snake’s Town on the Muskingum during Angus McDonald’s expedition; the musket ball lodged in his thigh near the groin and stayed there for the rest of his life. In the Revolution he was a lieutenant picked for Daniel Morgan’s riflemen and fought at Saratoga under Morgan. In April 1786 he settled his family on Pleasant Run, a branch of Beech Fork, about three miles east of present-day Springfield in what is now Washington County, Kentucky; the family farmed, raised livestock and joined the Methodist church. As a militia captain that year he attacked a Piankashaw village near Vincennes, although the Piankashaw were friendly to the Americans. Promoted to colonel, he led the Kentucky militia detachment routed in 1790 at Heller’s Corner—“Hardin’s Defeat”—which began a long run of American losses to the Miami chief Little Turtle, and in 1791 he led mounted militia against a Kickapoo village during Gen. Charles Scott’s Wabash campaign. In May 1792 Gen. James Wilkinson sent him to carry American peace terms to the nations along the Sandusky River. A Shawnee party offered to escort him, then killed him and his servant Freeman one night as he slept. Hardin County, Kentucky, and the town of Hardin, Ohio, near where he was killed, are named for him. His son Martin D. Hardin, later a U.S. senator from Kentucky, married Ann Logan, daughter of Gen. Benjamin Logan. The map pin is an approximate point about three miles east of Springfield, where the Kentucky Historical Society’s John Hardin marker stands on US 150 and where his son Mark Hardin placed the homestead; the exact house site is not mapped.

properties.name: Carrollton (Port William) at the Kentucky–Ohio confluence
properties.title: Carrollton (Port William) at the Kentucky–Ohio confluence
properties.subtitle: Carroll County · Point Park at the mouth of the Kentucky River · settled 1792 · incorporated as Port William 1794 · Gallatin County seat · renamed Carrollton 1838
properties.history: Where the Kentucky River empties into the Ohio, Gen. Charles Scott built a blockhouse in 1789 to protect settlers, according to the Kentucky Historical Society marker at Point Park. The town at the river mouth was first settled in 1792 and called Port William. Benjamin Craig, who had come to Kentucky with the Traveling Church led by his brother Lewis Craig, laid off the town on 613 acres that he and James Hawkins owned, and the legislature incorporated Port William in 1794; Craig had built the first brick house in the county in 1792. When Gallatin County was formed on December 14, 1798, from parts of Franklin and Shelby counties, Port William served as its county seat. The first Gallatin County court met on May 14, 1799, at the brick home of Richard and Sarah Masterson—leading Methodists, and Richard an early trustee of Port William—which still stands on the east side of town. In 1838 the Kentucky legislature formed Carroll County, partly out of Gallatin, and changed the town’s name to Carrollton, both in honor of Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the Maryland signer of the Declaration of Independence; Carrollton became the new county’s seat. The map pin marks Point Park at the confluence.

properties.name: Rowlandton Mound Site (15McN3), Paducah
properties.title: Rowlandton Mound Site (15McN3), Paducah
properties.subtitle: McCracken County · Paducah, oxbow lake edge south of the Ohio · Mississippian platform mound and village · occupation ~1100–1350 CE · pin rounded to 0.01°
properties.history: The Rowlandton Mound Site (15MCN3) is a Mississippian town site inside present-day Paducah, on the edge of an old oxbow lake a little south of the Ohio River. People lived there from about 1100 to about 1350 CE. The 3-hectare (7.4-acre) site has a large platform mound and an associated village area, roughly the size of the Wickliffe Mounds site in far western Kentucky. Archaeologists once thought that large civic centers in western Kentucky such as Rowlandton, Twin Mounds and Tolu were 13th-century expansions of the Kincaid Mounds polity in nearby southern Illinois, but excavations in 2006 by Kit Wesler of Murray State University showed that this was not the case; the centers were probably founded by local Late Woodland peoples. The map pin is the site’s published coordinate rounded to two decimals (about 1 km), the site’s rule for archaeological pins.

properties.name: Hidden River Cave (Horse Cave)
properties.title: Hidden River Cave (Horse Cave)
properties.subtitle: Hart County · sinkhole entrance at 119 E. Main St., Horse Cave · turbine 1890 · generator 1892 · tours 1912–1943 · American Cave Museum 1992
properties.history: Hidden River Cave lies directly beneath the town of Horse Cave in Hart County, and its main entrance is a large sinkhole at 119 East Main Street. The cave stream was the town’s water source, and attempts to set up public waterworks in the cave go back to 1879. Dentist George A. Thomas moved to Horse Cave in 1888, bought a house by the entrance and, a year later, bought the cave for $375. In 1890 a vertical-shaft turbine was built below the junction of the two cave streams to drive the pumps, and in 1892 an added electrical generator lit the Thomas home, his dental office and two other buildings—making Horse Cave, the cave’s operators say, the first town in Kentucky with incandescent lights (Louisville had electric arc lights earlier). The cave offered commercial tours from 1912 through 1943, though the same history dates the opening of a half-mile tour section to 1916. Domestic and industrial sewage dumped into sinkholes and wells fouled the stream; with noxious odors, low wartime visitation and a failed lawsuit, the tours closed in 1943, and the cave became known as one of the most polluted in America. A regional sewage treatment system stopped the sewage in December 1989, the stream began to recover, and in 1992 the American Cave Museum opened beside the entrance and the steps down to the underground river were rebuilt. Tours reached Sunset Dome again in 2020.

properties.name: Canewood, Gen. Charles Scott’s last home (KHS marker #116)
properties.title: Canewood, Gen. Charles Scott’s last home (KHS marker #116)
properties.subtitle: Clark County · KHS marker #116, KY 627 about 6½ mi N of Winchester · Scott in Kentucky 1785–1813 · Scott’s Landing/Petersburg near Versailles not mapped
properties.history: Revolutionary War general Charles Scott first saw Kentucky in 1785, coming down the Ohio to Limestone, and moved his family out in 1787 to land near present-day Versailles, where he built a two-story log house, a stockade, and a tobacco inspection warehouse at what became Scott's Landing. That June, Shawnee warriors killed his son Samuel as he crossed the Ohio in a canoe while Scott watched from the bank, and another son, Merritt, was killed in Harmar's 1790 campaign. Scott sold lots for a town he called Petersburg and offered it as the new state capital in 1792, but Frankfort won, and Petersburg never grew into a real town. In 1791 he led Kentucky mounted volunteers against the Wea towns on the Wabash. He went on to lead Kentucky's mounted volunteers under Anthony Wayne at Fallen Timbers in 1794, served as the fourth governor from 1808 to 1812, died at his Canewood estate in 1813, and was reburied in Frankfort Cemetery in 1854. Scott County and Scottsville are named for him. The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society's Canewood marker in Clark County, for the house Scott shared with his wife, the widow of Col. Nathaniel Gist, in his last years; the sites of Scott's Landing and Petersburg near Versailles are not mapped.

properties.name: Flemingsburg (Fleming County courthouse)
properties.title: Flemingsburg (Fleming County courthouse)
properties.subtitle: Fleming County · courthouse lawn, Flemingsburg (KHS marker #950) · Stockton’s Station 1787 · Fleming’s Station 1788 · county seat 1798 · incorporated 1812
properties.history: Col. John Fleming came into the hill country south of Limestone in 1776 to mark and improve land, served as an officer in the Revolution, and built Fleming's Station in 1788. It was the second fort in the area. The first was Stockton's Station, built in 1787 by his half-brother, Maj. George Stockton, who had raised a crop on the spot in 1786 while still living at Strode's Station. Stockton owned the land where the town grew, laid it out in the mid-1790s (the Kentucky Historical Society marker says 1796), and named it for his half-brother. When Fleming County was cut from Mason in 1798 as Kentucky's 26th county, Flemingsburg became its seat, and the legislature incorporated the town in 1812. The country stayed dangerous for years: Robert Stockton was killed by Indians in 1789 and still lies under stacked rock slabs in a field in eastern Fleming County. The map pin marks the Fleming County marker on the courthouse lawn in Flemingsburg.

George Stockton, who had raised a crop on the spot in 1786 while still living at Strode's Station. Stockton owned the land where the town grew, laid it out in the mid-1790s (the Kentucky Historical Society marker says 1796), and named it for his half-brother. When Fleming County was cut from Mason in 1798 as Kentucky's 26th county, Flemingsburg became its seat, and the legislature incorporated the town in 1812. The country stayed dangerous for years: Robert Stockton was killed by Indians in 1789 and still lies under stacked rock slabs in a field in eastern Fleming County. properties.name: Stitzel Brothers Distillery remains, 25th & Maple, Louisville
properties.title: Stitzel Brothers Distillery remains, 25th & Maple, Louisville
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · 2501 Maple St., western Louisville · Stitzel barrel-rack patent 1879 · Stitzel-Weller opens in Shively 1935
properties.history: Before 1879, Kentucky warehousemen rolled barrels into lines on the floor, laid a pair of wooden rails across them, and rolled another row on top, three or four barrels high. Reaching a bottom barrel meant taking the whole line apart, the weight made the lower barrels leak, and poor air flow could leave whiskey musty after a hot summer. Louisville distiller Frederick Stitzel, working on the problem at the Glencoe Distillery, patented a fix in 1879: timber frames with projecting rails, so every barrel rested on its own ledge with air all around it and any one could be rolled out without disturbing the rest. The racks stood free of the building's walls, and insurance maps of the era started labeling such buildings "patent warehouses." The rick system is still the standard in Kentucky rickhouses, and the family name carried on: the A. Ph. Stitzel Distillery later joined W. L. Weller & Sons, and Stitzel-Weller opened in Shively on Derby Day 1935. Stitzel’s racks came eighteen years before E. H. Taylor Jr.’s Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897. The map pin marks the surviving buildings of the Stitzel Brothers Distillery at 25th and Maple streets in western Louisville; the site of the Glencoe Distillery is not mapped.

properties.name: Jeptha’s Knob marker, Clay Village (KHS #161)
properties.title: Jeptha’s Knob marker, Clay Village (KHS #161)
properties.subtitle: Shelby County · KHS marker #161 at Clay Village @ Jeptha Knob Road · suspected impact structure · described 1887 (Linney), mapped 1925 (Bucher) · knob on private land
properties.history: About eight miles east of Shelbyville near Clay Village, Jeptha Knob rises some 300 feet above the surrounding farmland and is the highest point in the Bluegrass. Underneath is a circular structure nearly three miles across: a core of uplifted, shattered Ordovician limestone and shale ringed by concentric and radial faults, later buried under flat-lying Silurian rock. William Linney of the Kentucky Geological Survey first described it in 1887, and Walter Bucher mapped it in 1925 and called it "cryptovolcanic," the word still on its roadside marker. Most geologists now suspect a meteorite or comet strike around the end of the Ordovician, roughly 440 million years ago, and unusually high iridium in its broken rock points that way, but it isn't on the official list of impact craters because no shatter cones or coesite have been found. The knob is on private land. The years on this story are the human ones, from Linney’s 1887 report to Bucher’s 1925 map. The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society’s Jeptha’s Knob marker at Clay Village; the knob itself is private.

properties.name: Daniel Trabue House, Columbia (KHS marker #1782)
properties.title: Daniel Trabue House, Columbia (KHS marker #1782)
properties.subtitle: Adair County · 299 Jamestown St., Columbia · KHS marker #1782 · house built ca. 1823 · Trabue in Kentucky 1778–1840
properties.history: Daniel Trabue (1760–1840), raised in Chesterfield County, Virginia, and descended from French Huguenots, came through Cumberland Gap as a teenager with his brother James and spent nearly three years in Kentucky, at Fort Boonesborough and Logan’s Fort. He went back to Virginia, peddled goods to American soldiers during the Yorktown campaign, married Mary Haskins in 1782, and brought his family down the Ohio in 1785. After several years in Fayette County near the Kentucky River, the family moved to the Green River country in present Adair County. There Trabue helped survey and establish the town of Columbia and served as town trustee, sheriff, and justice of the peace while running a grist mill, an inn, and a store. About 1823 he built a brick house on a hill above town; money troubles forced the family out in 1828. In 1827 he wrote his memoir of the pioneer years, including events at Logan’s Station, Boonesborough, and service under Anthony Wayne. It survives in the Draper Manuscripts and is read today as Westward into Kentucky: The Narrative of Daniel Trabue. The map pin marks his house at 299 Jamestown Street in Columbia (KHS marker #1782).

properties.name: Russellville (Logan Court House), Logan County courthouse square
properties.title: Russellville (Logan Court House), Logan County courthouse square
properties.subtitle: Logan County · downtown Russellville at the courthouse square · Cook’s Station 1790 · Logan Court House 1792 · named for Gen. William Russell 1798 · established 1810
properties.history: The Logan County seat started as a spring with a string of names: Big Boiling Spring, Gasper Butcher’s Spring, Butcher’s Station. A local historian put Butcher there around 1780, but others have questioned it, and historian W. R. Jillson found no written record of anyone living on the site before 1790, when William Cook and his wife built Cook’s Cabin (Cook’s Station) about a mile east of today’s town, joined by 18-year-old William Stewart. The settlement became Logan Court House when it was picked as the seat of the new Logan County in 1792. Gen. William Russell, who held a 2,000-acre grant there for Revolutionary War service, donated land for the platted county seat in 1795; the town took his name in 1798, and the legislature formally established it on Jan. 15, 1810. The same county saw the Rev. James McGready’s June 1800 camp meeting at the Red River Meeting House, often counted as the start of the Revival of 1800, and Andrew Jackson’s fatal 1806 duel with Charles Dickinson at Harrison’s Mill. The map pin marks downtown Russellville at the courthouse square.

properties.name: Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve (Boone’s Overlook)
properties.title: Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve (Boone’s Overlook)
properties.subtitle: Powell County · Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve · Boone and Finley’s traditional first view of the Bluegrass, June 7, 1769 · preserve dedicated 1985
properties.history: Pilot Knob, a 730-foot sandstone outcrop in Powell County, is believed to be where Daniel Boone and John Finley first looked out over the Bluegrass. By tradition they reached the summit on June 7, 1769, before making camp and exploring the country beyond; Finley called it “the beautiful level of Kentucky,” and John Filson’s 1784 Boone narrative has Boone recalling that he “had gained the summit of a commanding ridge” and “beheld the ample plains, the beauteous tracts below.” The Kentucky Historical Society marks June 7 as Boone Day. The knob, also called Boone’s Overlook, is Pennsylvanian conglomerate sandstone, and pieces of it were once quarried for millstones. From the top you can see the Cumberland Plateau, the Knobs, and the Bluegrass. The state dedicated the first 308 acres as Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve on Sept. 26, 1985; it has since grown to about 1,258 acres with two strenuous trails. The map pin marks the preserve, near the knob.

properties.name: Red Bird River Petroglyphs, original site near Eriline (15CY51)
properties.title: Red Bird River Petroglyphs, original site near Eriline (15CY51)
properties.subtitle: Clay County · original cliff site above the Red Bird River near Eriline (generalized) · carvings undated · fell Dec. 7, 1994; now in Rawlings–Stinson Park, Manchester
properties.history: A 50-ton sandstone block cut with petroglyphs sat in a cliff above the Red Bird River near Eriline in Clay County. The inscribed face was about 5½ feet high and 20 feet long, with sharp, linear carvings that the authors of Rock Art of Kentucky called “different from any of the previously reported Kentucky petroglyphs.” Nobody has dated them: a state marker credits a legendary Cherokee chief named Red Bird, but the Kentucky Historical Society itself has said there are no reliable dates, and writers have described the marks as possibly Native, colonial, or both. That gap is why this story carries no years. The site, 15CY51, went on the National Register in September 1989. Building and widening KY 66 undercut the face, and on Dec. 7, 1994, the block fell onto the road at Lower Red Bird; two days later it was moved to Rawlings–Stinson Park in Manchester, where it sits roofed and fenced. It was taken off the Register in 2003. A sign at the park claims eight Old World alphabets on the stone, a fringe claim scholars reject. It isn’t the Red Bird River Shelter (15CY52) across the river. The map pin is the original riverside site, rounded to two decimals.

properties.name: McLean Drift Bank, old Paradise on the Green River (generalized)
properties.title: McLean Drift Bank, old Paradise on the Green River (generalized)
properties.subtitle: Muhlenberg County · Green River at the lost town of Paradise (generalized point) · first commercial coal mine in Kentucky 1820 · TVA buyout of Paradise 1967
properties.history: Explorer Thomas Walker found coal in what would become Kentucky in 1750 and burned it in his campfire, but nobody mined it for sale for another seventy years. In 1820 Kentucky’s first commercial coal mine, the McLean Drift Bank, opened along the Green River at what became the village of Paradise in Muhlenberg County, and it produced 328 tons in its first year. For decades the Western Coalfield carried the whole state: 100,000 tons by 1843 and a million tons by 1879, the year the first commercial mine in the Eastern Coalfield opened in Bell County. Paradise began as Stom’s Landing, named for Leonard Stom, who ran a ferry there, and it became a coal-mining town. The sources don’t say when the drift bank itself closed. TVA began building its Paradise coal plant on the town site in 1959, bought out the last residents in 1967, and demolished the town, which lives on in John Prine’s song “Paradise.” The exact mine site isn’t published, so the map pin is a generalized point at old Paradise.

properties.name: Gen. James Wilkinson’s Love House site, Frankfort (KHS marker #1182)
properties.title: Gen. James Wilkinson’s Love House site, Frankfort (KHS marker #1182)
properties.subtitle: Franklin County · Wapping & Wilkinson Sts., Frankfort · house built ca. 1786 by Wilkinson · Frankfort laid out 1786 · Spanish oath 1787 · Frankfort land sold 1792
properties.history: James Wilkinson (1757–1825), born in Maryland, was brevetted a brigadier general in November 1777, at 20, after carrying news of the Saratoga victory to Congress, though he was soon pushed to resign. He moved to Kentucky in 1784 and threw himself into the fight to separate from Virginia. He bought land at Frank’s Ford on the Kentucky River from Humphrey Marshall, won Virginia’s approval in 1786 to lay out a town there, and drew the street plan of what became Frankfort; about 1786 he also built the house later called the Love House, where the legislature first met in 1793. In April 1787 he made a trading trip down the Mississippi to New Orleans, capital of Spanish Louisiana, where Gov. Esteban Miró agreed to let Kentucky trade on the river in return for Wilkinson’s promise to serve Spanish interests. On Aug. 22, 1787, Wilkinson signed an expatriation declaration and swore allegiance to the King of Spain. His “First Memorial” urged Spain to take Kentuckians under its protection, and his letters were written in a cipher called “Number 13,” the source of his nickname, Agent 13. He chaired a committee at the November 1788 separation convention but could not swing it toward Spain, and in 1792 he sold his Frankfort land to Andrew Holmes. He went on to serve twice as the senior officer of the U.S. Army while still secretly taking Spanish money. Historian Charles Gayarré published his letters to Miró in 1854, proving what many had suspected. Theodore Roosevelt wrote that “in all our history, there is no more despicable character,” and Frederick Jackson Turner called him “the most consummate artist in treason that the nation ever possessed.” The map pin marks the site of the Love House at Wapping and Wilkinson streets in Frankfort (KHS marker #1182).

properties.name: Hodgenville (Hodgen’s Mill), KHS marker #1096
properties.title: Hodgenville (Hodgen’s Mill), KHS marker #1096
properties.subtitle: LaRue County · Hodgenville, KY 61 · Phillips Fort 1780 · Hodgen’s mill 1789 · town established Feb. 1818 · LaRue County seat 1843
properties.history: The LaRue County seat grew up around a gristmill. The county’s first settlement was Phillips Fort, built in 1780 on the North Fork of the Nolin River by surveyor Philip Phillips and a company of settlers from Pennsylvania; it served as a refuge from Indian raids until about 1786, when it was safe enough to build homes, and it was then abandoned and taken down. Robert Hodgen, a Pennsylvania-born tavern keeper who bought land in the area, built a gristmill on the Nolin in 1789 within the protection of the fort. After his death, his widow and children petitioned for a town, and in February 1818 the Hardin County Court established Hodgenville on 27 acres of Hodgen land. The post office opened in 1826 (spelled Hodgensville until 1904), the town incorporated in 1839, and when LaRue County was formed from Hardin County on March 1, 1843, Hodgenville became its seat. In between, on Feb. 12, 1809, Abraham Lincoln was born in a cabin on Sinking Spring Farm a few miles south. For the centennial of his birth, Adolph Weinman’s bronze seated Lincoln was dedicated on the town square on May 31, 1909, with Robert Todd Lincoln in the crowd of more than 10,000. The map pin marks the KHS Hodgenville marker (#1096) in town.

properties.name: Warriors’ Path (Athiamiowee), KHS marker #697, Gray Hawk
properties.title: Warriors’ Path (Athiamiowee), KHS marker #697, Gray Hawk
properties.subtitle: Jackson County · US 421 at Gray Hawk; the path ran along War Fork two miles east · Shawnee–Cherokee trail · travelers 1674–1769
properties.history: Long before the Wilderness Road, the main north–south route through eastern Kentucky was a Native trail the Shawnee called Athiamiowee, the “Path of the Armed Ones.” It linked the Shawnee and other nations north of the Ohio with the Cherokee towns of east Tennessee and the southern Appalachians. Like most Native routes it followed old game trails worn by elk and buffalo through gaps and valleys, and it was marked or blazed along the way. The Shawnee and Cherokee, often bitter enemies, both used it to reach the Kentucky hunting grounds and to raid each other, and English speakers were calling it the Warriors’ Path by the 1750s. In Kentucky it came north through Cumberland Gap, crossed the Cumberland River at Cumberland Ford (present Pineville), followed the river toward Flat Lick, then ran overland to Goose Creek in Clay County and along War Fork in Jackson County. It crossed Powell County and part of Clark County near the Shawnee town of Eskippakithiki, crossed the Licking River near Blue Licks, and reached the Ohio at Cabin Creek in Mason County. Gabriel Arthur followed it in 1674 after his Native captors released him, and Thomas Walker in 1750, Christopher Gist in 1751, and John Finley with Daniel Boone in 1769 all used it; John Filson’s 1784 map of Kentucky shows it. A Kentucky Historical Society marker (#697) on US 421 at Gray Hawk notes that the path ran along War Fork two miles east, and the map pin marks that marker.

properties.name: Old Fort Earthworks (15Gp1), Portsmouth Earthworks Group A (generalized)
properties.title: Old Fort Earthworks (15Gp1), Portsmouth Earthworks Group A (generalized)
properties.subtitle: Greenup County · near South Portsmouth (generalized point) · Middle Woodland square enclosure, about 200 BC–AD 500
properties.history: Across the Ohio River from Portsmouth, Ohio, near South Portsmouth in Greenup County, Middle Woodland builders (about 200 BC to AD 500) raised the westernmost part of the Portsmouth Earthworks. Old Fort Earthworks (site 15Gp1) is a square earthen enclosure on a terrace above the Ohio floodplain. It surrounds 13.5 acres; its north and south walls run 825 feet and its east and west walls 822 feet, and its corners, not its walls, point to the four cardinal directions. Pairs of long, low parallel embankments, the “arms,” run out from the east and west walls, and walled roads once tied this group to the rest of the complex across the river, which E. G. Squier mapped in 1847. In 1774 a surveying party under Hanson, laying off land at the mouth of the Scioto for Patrick Henry, noted the enclosure in their journal and wrongly guessed it was the ruin of a 1750s stone trading house. WPA crews mapped and trenched it in 1938, the only systematic excavation, and found how the walls were built: the builders left the old topsoil in place, spread about two feet of nearby soil and humus over it, heaped thousands of basketloads of sand, gravel, loam, and clay into a six-foot core, then dressed the slope with yellow-brown clay. They also filled ravines and cut slopes to keep the walls level, and they and later Native groups kept the interior clean. It was listed on the National Register on Dec. 4, 1980, as Portsmouth Earthworks, Group A. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey does not publish site locations, so the map pin is the National Register point rounded to two decimals.
properties.description: Across the Ohio River from Portsmouth, Ohio, near South Portsmouth in Greenup County, Middle Woodland builders (about 200 BC to AD 500) raised the westernmost part of the Portsmouth Earthworks. Old Fort Earthworks (site 15Gp1) is a square earthen enclosure on a terrace above the Ohio floodplain. It surrounds 13.5 acres; its north and south walls run 825 feet and its east and west walls 822 feet, and its corners, not its walls, point to the four cardinal directions. Pairs of long, low parallel embankments, the “arms,” run out from the east and west walls, and walled roads once tied this group to the rest of the complex across the river, which E. G. Squier mapped in 1847. In 1774 a surveying party under Hanson, laying off land at the mouth of the Scioto for Patrick Henry, noted the enclosure in their journal and wrongly guessed it was the ruin of a 1750s stone trading house. WPA crews mapped and trenched it in 1938, the only systematic excavation, and found how the walls were built: the builders left the old topsoil in place, spread about two feet of nearby soil and humus over it, heaped thousands of basketloads of sand, gravel, loam, and clay into a six-foot core, then dressed the slope with yellow-brown clay. They also filled ravines and cut slopes to keep the walls level, and they and later Native groups kept the interior clean. It was listed on the National Register on Dec. 4, 1980, as Portsmouth Earthworks, Group A. properties.name: Cane Ridge Meeting House (KHS marker #51)
properties.title: Cane Ridge Meeting House (KHS marker #51)
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County · Cane Ridge, about 6 mi. east of Paris · log meeting house 1791 · camp meeting Aug. 1801 · Springfield Presbytery dissolved 1804
properties.history: About six miles east of Paris in Bourbon County, Presbyterian settlers built a meeting house of blue ash logs in 1791 on a ridge named for its canebrakes. Enslaved worshippers sat in a gallery reached by an outside ladder at the west end until an 1829 renovation removed it. Barton W. Stone began preaching at Cane Ridge in 1796. In August 1801 the congregation invited neighboring Presbyterian and Methodist churches to its annual communion, and from Aug. 6 to Aug. 12 or 13 the crowds kept coming. Estimates run from 10,000 to 20,000 or more; The Encyclopedia of the Stone-Campbell Movement figures that 20,000 could have come at some point during the week, nearly a tenth of Kentucky’s 1800 population, though probably no more than 10,000 at once. Eighteen Presbyterian ministers and numerous Methodists and Baptists preached, often at the same time in different parts of the camp, from the meeting house, outdoor platforms, stumps, wagons, and fallen trees, and 800 to 1,100 people took communion. It was the largest and most famous camp meeting of the Second Great Awakening and set off a wave of smaller camp meetings across the frontier. In 1804 Stone and other Presbyterian ministers signed “The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery” at Cane Ridge (the state marker dates the new “Christian Church” to June 28, 1804), starting a movement that joined Thomas and Alexander Campbell’s followers in 1832. In the 1930s a stone building was put up around the original log meeting house, which still stands inside it. The map pin marks the meeting house.

properties.name: John Bradford’s Fairfield, KHS marker #1864 (Kentucky Gazette printer)
properties.title: John Bradford’s Fairfield, KHS marker #1864 (Kentucky Gazette printer)
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · 1916 Iron Works Pike, north of Lexington · Kentucke Gazette first printed Aug. 11, 1787 · Transylvania board chair 1793–1830
properties.history: John Bradford (1749–1830), born in Prince William County, Virginia, first came to Kentucky with a surveying party in 1775 and moved his family out in 1784 or 1785. He had little experience as a printer or editor, but with Fielding Bradford he started Kentucky’s first newspaper in Lexington, the Kentucke Gazette. The first issue was printed on Aug. 11, 1787, and the paper switched to the modern spelling of the state’s name in 1789. It had no rival within 500 miles until 1795. After statehood, Bradford printed the first book published in Kentucky, a compilation of the acts of the legislature’s first session in 1792. He served as a Lexington town trustee, in the legislature, and as Fayette County sheriff, and he helped found Transylvania University, chairing its board of trustees from 1793 until his death in 1830. Beginning in August 1828 he wrote a series of 66 newspaper articles on Kentucky’s early years: the Indian wars, the fight for free use of the Mississippi and the port of New Orleans, and the ten conventions that led to statehood. Those “Notes” are still a valued source on the era. On his farm north of Lexington he built a Flemish-bond brick house called Fairfield, about 1785–1800. The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society’s John Bradford marker (#1864) at 1916 Iron Works Pike.

properties.name: Carlisle courthouse square (Nicholas County seat since 1816)
properties.title: Carlisle courthouse square (Nicholas County seat since 1816)
properties.subtitle: Nicholas County · Main St., Carlisle · county formed 1799 · seat at Ellisville 1805 · Kincart’s 50-acre gift and new seat 1816
properties.history: Nicholas County was formed in 1799 from parts of Mason and Bourbon counties and named for Col. George Nicholas, a Revolutionary War veteran who became a popular lawyer in early Kentucky. Its county court first met in 1800 at the home of Martin Baker Jr. at Lower Blue Licks, then in a new courthouse at Blue Licks. In 1805 the seat moved to a new town, Ellisville, laid out on James Ellis’s farm along the Lexington–Maysville road, where the county’s courthouse stood until 1816. That year the seat moved again. John Kincart, born in 1791 in what became Nicholas County, had inherited his father Samuel’s 200-acre farm in 1813, and in 1816 he gave 50 acres, including the family’s peach orchard, for a new town named Carlisle. Streets and lots were laid off around the center of the tract, and Kincart took town lots as payment for his land. The present Nicholas County Courthouse is the third on that site, and a monument to Samuel Kincart stands on its north side. Daniel Boone had lived in the county from 1795 to 1799, and his restored cabin in Carlisle is kept by the Carlisle Tourism Commission. The map pin marks the courthouse square.

properties.name: Kentucky Association race course site, E. Fifth & Race Sts., Lexington
properties.title: Kentucky Association race course site, E. Fifth & Race Sts., Lexington
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · East End, Lexington · Association formed July 23, 1826 · track land bought 1828–1834 · Phoenix Hotel Handicap 1831 · closed 1933
properties.history: On July 23, 1826, Bluegrass horsemen formed the Kentucky Association to promote the breeding and racing of Thoroughbreds. Its founders included Henry Clay, Jesse Bledsoe, Dr. Elisha Warfield, and Thomas F. Marshall, and the Keeneland Library’s account says about fifty members met at Mrs. Keen’s Inn with the aim “to improve the breed of horses by encouraging the sports of the turf.” Between 1828 and 1834 the Association bought 65 acres at what is now the east end of Fifth Street at Race Street in Lexington and built the Lexington Race Course, a one-mile dirt track with a grandstand and stables. The Phoenix Hotel Handicap was first run there in 1831; as the Phoenix Stakes it is now the oldest stakes race in the United States. Lexington’s racing had long depended on enslaved grooms, trainers, and riders, and after emancipation Black horsemen stayed central at the track: future Hall of Fame jockey Isaac Murphy won his first race there on Sept. 16, 1876, and Jimmy Winkfield got his start there in 1898. Money troubles forced a sale in 1890. The Association closed the track in the spring of 1933, the same spring the Keeneland Association incorporated to build a new course outside town, and the old grounds were torn down in 1935. Keeneland copied the old track’s gates. The site is now part of Lexington’s East End, around William Wells Brown Elementary School, where street names recall the track. The map pin marks the Fifth and Race streets area.

properties.name: Mantle Rock, Trail of Tears campsite (KHS marker #1675)
properties.title: Mantle Rock, Trail of Tears campsite (KHS marker #1675)
properties.subtitle: Livingston County · KY 133, about 3 mi. west of Joy; the arch is ½ mile from the marker · Cherokee detachments camped here winter 1838–39
properties.history: West of the crossroads of Joy in Livingston County, off KY 133, a sandstone arch about 30 feet high and 188 feet long stands in the woods of the McGilligan Creek watershed, one of the longest natural arches in Kentucky. Nearby runs a stretch of the old Salem–Golconda Road, and in the winter of 1838–39 that road carried the Cherokee Nation’s forced removal on the northern route of the Trail of Tears. Eleven detachments, more than 10,000 Cherokee in all, came this way toward Berry’s Ferry on the Ohio and the crossing to Golconda, Illinois, not yet halfway to Indian Territory. Ice closed the river that winter. The Peter Hildebrand detachment, about 1,766 people, spent roughly two bitterly cold weeks in camps strung for miles along the road, waiting for the river to thaw enough for the ferry. A state historical marker says the Cherokee sheltered beneath the arch and that many died there; the National Park Service says there were far too many people to camp under it, that historical descriptions point to a long camp along the road, and that there is no evidence of burials at Mantle Rock. Across the river, many were trapped again between the frozen Ohio and Mississippi, and the detachments reached Oklahoma hundreds fewer than they started. The Nature Conservancy owns the 367-acre preserve. It was listed on the National Register in 2004 as the Mantle Rock Archeological District and certified that year as a site on the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, and a 2.75-mile loop trail follows about a mile of the old road. The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society’s Mantle Rock marker (#1675) on KY 133.
